{{Use Australian English|date=July 2018}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2018}}
[[File:Showing method of attack with boomerang - NMA-15147.jpg|thumb|312x312px|right|Aboriginal man with shield and boomerang]]
[[File:Aboriginal child asleep in a wooden dish, central Australia, ca. 1940s (8718150313).jpg|238x238px|thumb|right|Child asleep in wooden dish, central Australia, c.1940s]]
'''Australian Aboriginal artefacts''' include a variety of [[cultural artefact]]s used by [[Aboriginal Australians]]. Most Aboriginal artefacts were multi-purpose and could be used for a variety of different occupations. Spears, [[Waddy|clubs]], [[boomerang]]s and [[Hielaman|shields]] were used generally as weapons for hunting and in warfare. Watercraft technology artefacts in the form of [[Dugout canoe|dugout]] and bark canoes were used for transport and for fishing. Stone artefacts include cutting tools and grinding stones to hunt and make food. [[Coolamon (vessel)|Coolamons]] and carriers such as [[dillybag]]s, allowed Aboriginal peoples to carry water, food and cradle babies. [[Message stick]]s were used for communication, and ornamental artefacts for decorative and ceremonial purposes. Aboriginal children’s toys were used to both entertain and educate.

== Weapons ==

Aboriginal peoples used several different types of weapons including [[shield]]s (also known as [[hielaman]]), spears, [[spear-thrower]]s, [[boomerang]]s and clubs. Peoples from different regions used different weapons.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Aboriginal Australia|date=1981|publisher=Australian Gallery Directors Council|others=Cooper, Carol., National Gallery of Victoria., Australian Gallery Directors' Council.|isbn=0-642-89689-5|location=Sydney|oclc=8487510}}</ref> Some peoples, for example, would fight with boomerangs and shields, whereas in another region they would fight with clubs. Weapons could be used both for hunting game and in warfare.<ref>{{cite web |title=Aboriginal weapon Spear throwers |url=https://www.aboriginal-bark-paintings.com/aboriginal-weapons/#:~:text=These%20are%20spears%2C%20spear%20throwers,and%20clubs%20were%20for%20warfare. |website=ABORIGINAL BARK PAINTINGS |date = 29 August 2017|access-date=30 May 2021}}</ref>
[[File:Two men with wooden hair ornaments, spears and shields, photograph by H. Basedow.jpg|206x206px|right|thumb|Aboriginal men with spears and shields]]
Weapons were of different styles in different areas. For example, a shield from [[Central Australia]] is very different from a shield from [[North Queensland]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aboriginal-bark-paintings.com/aboriginal-weapons/|title=aboriginal weapons {{!}} Aborigines weapons {{!}} sell aboriginal weapons|date=2017-08-29|website=Aboriginal Bark Paintings|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref>

=== Spears ===
Aboriginal peoples used [[spear]]s for a variety of purposes including hunting, fishing, gathering fruit, fighting, retribution, punishment, in [[Aboriginal Australian ceremony|ceremony]], as commodities for trade, and as symbolic markers of [[masculine gender|masculinity]].<ref name="Allen2015">{{cite journal |last1=Allen |first1=H |last2=Akerman |first2=K |title=Innovation and change in northern Australian Aboriginal spear technologies: the case for reed spears |journal=Archaeology in Oceania |date=2015 |volume=50 |pages=83–93 |doi=10.1002/arco.5051 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Nugent2015">{{cite journal |last1=Nugent |first1=S |title=Sticks and stones: a functional analysis of Aboriginal spears from Northern Australia |journal=The University of Queensland |date=2015 }}</ref><ref name="Akerman2002">{{cite journal |last1=Akerman |first1=Kim |last2=Fullagar |first2=Richard |last3=van Gijn |first3=Annelou |title=Weapons and Wunan: Production, Function and Exchange of Kimberley Points |journal=Australian Aboriginal Studies |date=2002 |volume=2002 |issue=1 |pages=13–42 }}</ref> Spears were historically used by skilful hand-throwing, but with changes in Aboriginal spear technologies during the [[Holocene|mid-Holocene]], they could be thrown further and with more accuracy with the aid of [[spear-thrower]] projectiles.<ref name="Allen2015" /><ref name="Nugent2015" /> Spears could be made from a variety of materials including [[softwood]]s, bamboo (''[[Bambusa arnhemica]]''), cane and reed.<ref name="Allen2015" /> Projectile points could also be made from many different materials including [[Lithic flake|flaked stone]], shell, wood, kangaroo or wallaby bone, lobster claws, stingray spines, fish teeth, and more recently iron, glass and ceramics.<ref name="Allen2015" /><ref name="Nugent2015" /><ref name="Akerman2002" /><ref name="Attenbrow2021">{{cite web |last1=Attenbrow |first1=Val |title=Fishing spears, callarr, mooting |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/sydney/fishing-spears-callarr-mooting/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=12 May 2021}}</ref> These spear points could be bound to the spear using [[Mastic (plant resin)|mastics]], glues, gum, string, [[plant fibre]] and [[sinew]]s.<ref name="Allen2015" /><ref name="Nugent2015" /><ref name="Attenbrow2021" />

=== Clubs ===
An Aboriginal club, otherwise known as a [[waddy]] or nulla-nulla, could be used for a variety of purposes such as for hunting, fishing, digging, for grooving tools, warfare and in ceremonies.<ref name="MBANTUA2021">{{cite web |title=Weapons |url=https://mbantua.com.au/weapons/ |publisher=MBANTUA |access-date=26 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="nullanulla2021">{{cite web |title=nulla nulla |url=https://victoriancollections.net.au/items/51bbc5692162ef16005cf3a8 |website=victoriancollections.net.au |publisher=Victorian Collections |access-date=26 May 2021}}</ref>  A fighting club, called a ‘Lil-lil’, could, with a heavy blow, break a leg, rib or skull. Clubs which could create severe trauma were made from extremely hard woods such as [[acacia]]s including [[Acacia estrophiolata|ironwood]] and [[Acacia oswaldii|mitji]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Westaway |first1=Michael |last2=Williams |first2=Douglas |last3=Wright |first3=Richard |last4=Wood |first4=Rachel |last5=Olley |first5=Jon |last6=Swift |first6=Jaime |last7=Martin |first7=Sarah |last8=Kemp |first8=Justine |last9=Rolton |first9=Shane |last10=Bates |first10=William |title=The death of Kaakutja: A case of peri-mortem weapon trauma in an Aboriginal man from north-western New South Wales, Australia |journal=Antiquity |year=2016 |volume=90 |issue=353 |pages=1318–1333 |doi=10.15184/aqy.2016.173 |s2cid=164120825 }}</ref> Many clubs were fire hardened and others had sharpened stone quartz attached to the handle with [[spinifex resin]].<ref name="MBANTUA2021" />

=== Boomerangs ===
[[File:Yuendumu Gold 13.jpg|right|thumb|212x212px|Aboriginal man with boomerang, near [[Yuendumu]]]]
The [[boomerang]] is recognised by many as a significant cultural symbol of Australia.<ref name="NMA2021">{{cite web |title=Earliest evidence of the boomerang in Australia |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/earliest-evidence-of-the-boomerang-in-australia#:~:text=A%2023%2C000%2Dyear%2Dold%20mammoth,to%20about%2010%2C000%20years%20ago. |website=National Museum Australia |access-date=27 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="Philip1996">{{cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Philip |title=Boomerang: behind an Australian icon |date=1996 |publisher=Wakefield press |isbn=978-1862543829}}</ref> The term 'returning boomerang' is used to distinguish between ordinary boomerangs and the small percentage which, when thrown, will return to its thrower.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Akira |first1=Azuma |last2=Beppu |first2=Goro |last3=Ishikawa |first3=Hiroaki |last4=Yasuda |first4=Kunio |title=Flight dynamics of the boomerang, part 1: fundamental analysis |journal=Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics |date=2004 |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=545–554 |doi=10.2514/1.11157 |bibcode=2004JGCD...27..545A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sutherland |first1=Davidson |title=Is the boomerang oriental? |journal=Journal of the American Oriental Society |date=1935 |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=163–181 |doi=10.2307/594439 |jstor=594439 }}</ref> The oldest wooden boomerang artefact known in Australia, excavated from the Wyrie Swamp, [[South Australia]] in 1973, is estimated to be 9,500 years old.<ref name="NMA2021" />

Boomerangs could be used:
* as hunting or fighting weapons;<ref name="Aboriginal Weapons">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mbantua.com.au/aboriginal-weapons/|title=Aboriginal Weapons|website=www.mbantua.com.au|access-date=2018-04-01}}</ref>
* for digging;
* as cutting knives;<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://australianmuseum.net.au/hunting-boomerang-a-weapon-of-choice|title=Hunting Boomerang: a Weapon of Choice – Australian Museum|website=australianmuseum.net.au|language=en|access-date=2018-04-01}}</ref>
* for making fire by friction;<ref name="Aboriginal Weapons"/> and
* as percussion instruments for making music.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://austhrutime.com/weapons.htm|title=Aboriginal Weapons and Tools|website=austhrutime.com|access-date=2018-04-01}}</ref>

=== Shields ===
[[File:Aboriginal shields NGV.jpg|200x200px|thumb|Aboriginal shields from Ian Potter Centre]]
Shields were mainly used by Aboriginal warriors to defend themselves in dispute battles, often for [[Commodity (type of good)|commodities]] such as territory. A shield which had not lost a battle was thought to be inherently powerful and was a prized possession. Shields were made from wood or bark and usually had carved markings or painted designs. They could also be used in ceremonies such as in [[corroboree]]s.<ref name="Shields2021">{{cite web |title=Australian Aboriginal Shields |url=https://joyofmuseums.com/museums/australasia-museums/australian-museums/museums-of-sydney/australian-museum/australian-aboriginal-shields/#:~:text=Australian%20Aboriginal%20Shields%20were%20made,black%20design%20using%20natural%20pigments. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190406170158/https://joyofmuseums.com/museums/australasia-museums/australian-museums/museums-of-sydney/australian-museum/australian-aboriginal-shields/#:~:text=Australian%20Aboriginal%20Shields%20were%20made,black%20design%20using%20natural%20pigments. |url-status=usurped |archive-date=6 April 2019 |website=Joy of Museums Virtual Tours |publisher=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>

Aboriginal shields come in two main types: broad shields, and parrying shields. Parrying shields parry blows from a club whereas broad shields block spears. Shields for parrying are thick, strong and narrow, whereas broad shields are wide but thin. Aboriginal shields were made from different materials in different areas, they were made from buttress root, mulga wood, and bark. A handle is attached or carved on the back and the shield was often painted with red and white patterns. Arragong and Tawarrang shields were carved of wood often with an outer layer of bark. Tawarrang shields were notably narrow and long and had patterns carved into the sides. This particular category of shield could also be used as a musical instrument when struck with a club, in addition to its use as a weapon.<ref name="Attenbrow2014">{{cite journal |last1=Attenbrow |first1=V |last2=Cartwright |first2=C |title=An Aboriginal shield collected in 1770 at Kamay Botany Bay: an indicator of pre-colonial exchange systems in south-eastern Australia. |journal=Antiquity |date=2014 |volume=88 |issue=341 |pages=833–895 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00050754 |s2cid=162933814 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Nugent2018">{{cite journal |last1=Nugent |first1=M |last2=Sculthorpe |first2=G |title=A Shield Loaded with History: Encounters, Objects and Exhibitions |journal=Australian Historical Studies |date=2018 |volume=1 |pages=28–43 |doi=10.1080/1031461X.2017.1408663 |s2cid=149036662 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/1031461X.2017.1408663 |access-date=11 May 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Elemong shield is made from bark and is oval in shape. A handle is attached to the back and the shield was often painted with red and white patterns. Arragong and Tawarrang shields were carved of wood often with an outer layer of bark. Tawarrang shields were notably narrow and long and had patterns carved into the sides. This particular category of shield could also be used as a musical instrument when struck with a club, in addition to its use as a weapon.<ref name="Attenbrow2014">{{cite journal |last1=Attenbrow |first1=V |last2=Cartwright |first2=C |title=An Aboriginal shield collected in 1770 at Kamay Botany Bay: an indicator of pre-colonial exchange systems in south-eastern Australia. |journal=Antiquity |date=2014 |volume=88 |issue=341 |pages=833–895 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00050754 |s2cid=162933814 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Nugent2018">{{cite journal |last1=Nugent |first1=M |last2=Sculthorpe |first2=G |title=A Shield Loaded with History: Encounters, Objects and Exhibitions |journal=Australian Historical Studies |date=2018 |volume=1 |pages=28–43 |doi=10.1080/1031461X.2017.1408663 |s2cid=149036662 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/1031461X.2017.1408663 |access-date=11 May 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Shields originating from the [[North Queensland]] rainforest region are highly sought after by collectors due to their lavish decorative painting designs. These shields were made from [[buttress roots]] of rainforest [[fig trees]] (Ficus sp.) They were painted with red, yellow, white and black using natural materials including [[ochre]], [[clay]], [[charcoal]] and human blood. Shields from the post-contact period can, in some instances, include the colour blue. A piece of lawyer cane (''[[Calamus australis]]'') would be pushed up the shield owner's nose to cause bleeding. Blood would be put onto the shield, signifying their life being shared with the object. Designs on each shield were original and would represent the owners’ totemic affiliations and their country. This could be done through symbolism, composition and other means of visual representation. On the final day of a young Aboriginal man's initiation ceremony, he is given a blank shield for which he can create his own design. It was believed that the shield harnessed the power and protection of the owners [[totem]] and ancestral spirits.<ref name="Hayward2020">{{cite journal |last1=Hayward |first1=A |title=Two rare shield depictions from the Burrungkuy rock art region of Western Arnhem Land, Australia |journal=Australian Archaeology |date=2020 |volume=86 |issue=3 |pages=253–263|doi=10.1080/03122417.2020.1812796 |s2cid=225246370 }}</ref>

{{Blockquote
|text=The shield is a form of embodied knowledge that acts as substitute for the human body – a symbol not only of the person in his entirety but also a symbol of his expanded self, that is, his relationships with others. The shield covers the entire body, protects the body, is painted by and with the body (blood) and links the body (through totemic design) to clan..
|author=John Hayward
|title="Two rare shield depictions from the Burrungkuy rock art region of Western Arnhem Land, Australia"
|source=''Australian Archaeology'' (2020, Aug 17)
}}

The Australian Museum holds one of the wooden shields originating from the [[Kuku Yalanji]] people of the [[Daintree Rainforest]] on [[Cape York Peninsula|Cape York, Queensland]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Wooden Shield from Cape York, c1893 |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/australian-archaeology/wooden-shield-from-cape-york-c1893/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>
|-
| [[The British Museum]] || One of the most significant and earliest surviving Australian Aboriginal shield artefacts is widely believed [[File:Bark shield 2008 british museum.jpg|205x205px|thumb|upright|The Gweagal Shield 1770]]to have been collected by [[Captain Cook]] in 1770 during his first expedition (1768–71) to Australia. Known as the [[Gweagal shield]], it is {{convert|0.97|m|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.29|m|abbr=on}} wide and the bark has indentations on the surface, notably an obvious hole in the centre.<ref name="Attenbrow2014" /> [[Radiology|Radiographic]] images and scientific studies reveal that this was not a result of natural occurrences. The hole is believed, but not proven, to have been caused by a firearm during Cook’s attempt to make way to shore in April 1770.<ref name="Nugent2018" /> The artefact was transported back to England and is now on display in the [[British Museum]] in Cabinet 96 in the Enlightenment Gallery as Oc1978, Q.839.<ref name="Nugent2018" /><ref name="Hurley2020">{{cite journal |last1=Hurley |first1=W |title=Reports, silences and repercussion: wondering about the ballistic biography of the Leichhardt gunplate |journal=Rethinking History |date=2020 |volume=4 |issue=3–4 |pages=543–560|doi=10.1080/13642529.2020.1845536 |hdl=10453/144496 |s2cid=229409411 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It is regarded as a rare item which holds deep historical, scientific and social significance for indigenous and non-indigenous people. For this reason, the shield is a part of the “[[A History of the World in 100 Objects]]” project as Object 89.<ref name="Nugent2018" />

== Watercraft ==
[[File:Canoe making.jpg|236x236px|thumb|right|Aboriginal bark canoe making]]
Types of watercraft differed among Aboriginal communities, the most notable including bark canoes and dugout canoes which were built and used in different ways.<ref name="Gapps2015">{{cite journal |last1=Gapps |first1=S |last2=Smith |first2=M |title=Nawi – exploring Australia's Indigenous watercraft |journal=AlterNative|volume=2 |pages=87–102 }}</ref> Methods of constructing canoes were passed down through word of mouth in Aboriginal communities, not written or drawn. Canoes were used for fishing, hunting and as transport.<ref name="Payne2021">{{cite web |last1=Payne |first1=David |title=Indigenous Watercraft of Australia |url=http://arhv.anmm.gov.au/people/11358 |website=Australian National Maritime Museum |access-date=13 May 2021}}</ref>

=== Bark canoes ===
{{main article|Scarred tree}}
Bark canoes were most commonly made from [[List of Eucalyptus species|Eucalypt species]] including the bark of swamp she-oak [[Casuarina glauca]], [[Eucalyptus botryoides]], stringybark [[Eucalyptus agglomerata]] and [[Eucalyptus acmenoides]].<ref name="Wheeler2021">{{cite web |last1=Wheeler |first1=Helen |title=Bark canoe from New South Wales|url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/cultural-objects/indigenous-bark-canoe-from-new-south-wales/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=13 May 2021}}</ref>  Bark could only be successfully extracted at the right time of a wet season in order to limit the damage to the tree's growth and so that it was flexible enough to use. The bark would be cut with axes and peeled from the tree. More than one piece of bark was sometimes used.<ref name="Payne2021" /> "[[Scarred tree|Canoe trees]]" can be distinguished today due to their distinctive scars.<ref name="Wheeler2021" /> The shaping was done by a combination of heating with fire and soaking with water.<ref name="Payne2021" /> The ends of the bark canoe would be fastened with plant-fibre string with the bow (front of canoe) fastened to a point.<ref name="Wheeler2021" /> Branches could be used to reinforce joints; and clay, mud or other resin could be used to seal them.<ref name="Gapps2015" /> Due to the small [[Draft (hull)|draft]] and lightness of bark canoes, they were used in calmer waters such as [[billabong]]s, rivers, lakes, [[Estuaries of Australia|estuaries]] and bays.<ref name="Bradley1991" /> Aboriginal men would throw spears to catch fish from the canoe, whereas women would use hooks and lines. Bark paddles could be used to propel the canoe<ref name="Wheeler2021" /> and thick leafy branches were held to catch the wind.<ref name="Bradley1991" />

=== Dugout canoes ===
[[Aboriginal dugout canoe|Dugout canoes]] were a major development in watercraft technology and were suited for the open sea and in rougher conditions. They could be used for hunting [[dugongs]] and [[sea turtles]].<ref name="Bradley1991">{{cite journal |last1=Bradley |first1=J |title=Yanyuwa bark canoes: A brief survey of their use by the Yanyuwa people of the south western Gulf of Carpentaria |journal=Great Circle |date=1991 |volume=2 |pages=85–96 }}</ref>

== Stone artefacts ==
[[File:Aboriginal grain grinding. Uluru, (Ayers Rock), Australia.jpg|194x194px|thumb|Aboriginal grain grinding]]
{{further|Stone tool#Aboriginal Australian use}}
[[File:Australian Aboriginal stone artefacts.pdf|thumb|Stone artefacts scattered on the ground, Paroo River, Central Queensland.]]
Cutting tools made of stone and [[grindstone|grinding or pounding stones]] were also used as everyday items by Aboriginal peoples.<ref name="Hayes2018">{{cite journal |last1=Hayes |first1=E |last2=Fullagar |first2=R |last3=Mulvaney |first3=K |last4=Connell |first4=K |title=Food or fibercraft? Grinding stones and Aboriginal use of Triodia grass (spinifex). |journal=Quaternary International |date=2018 |volume=468 |pages=271–283 |doi=10.1016/j.quaint.2016.08.010 |bibcode=2018QuInt.468..271H |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.quaint.2016.08.010 |access-date=14 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Holdaway2012">{{cite journal |last1=Holdaway |first1=Simon |last2=Douglass |first2=Matthew |title=A Twenty-First Century Archaeology of Stone Artifacts |journal=Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory |date=2012 |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=101–131 |doi=10.1007/s10816-011-9103-6 |s2cid=162390339 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10816-011-9103-6 |access-date=14 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Cutting tools were made by hammering a core stone into [[lithic flake|flakes]].<ref name="Holdaway2012" /><ref name="McLaren2018">{{cite journal |last1=McLaren |first1=Andrew |last2=Oakes |first2=G |last3=Atkinson |first3=L |last4=Jordan |first4=D |last5=Toms |first5=P |title=Mid-to-Late Holocene Aboriginal Flakednoah Stone Artefact Technology on the Cumberland Plain, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia: A View from the South Creek Catchment |journal=Lithic Technology |date=2018 |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=202–227 |doi=10.1080/01977261.2018.1497116 |s2cid=134430151 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/01977261.2018.1497116 |access-date=11 May 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Grinding stones can include [[millstone]]s and [[Stone and muller|mullers]].<ref name="Grindstones2021">{{cite web |title=Grindstones |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/cultural-objects/grindstones/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=14 April 2021}}</ref> [[Quartzite]] is one of the main materials Aboriginal people used to create flakes but slate and other hard stone materials were also used.<ref name="Holdaway2012" /><ref name="Leilira2021">{{cite web |title=Leilira blades from Arnhem Land |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/cultural-objects/leilira-blades-from-arnhem-land/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=14 April 2021}}</ref><ref name="Law2020">{{cite journal |last1=Law |first1=W |last2=Slack |first2=M |title=The Story is in the Rocks: How Stone Artifact Scatters can Inform our Understanding of Ancient Aboriginal Stone Arrangement Functions |journal=Journal of Field Archaeology |date=2020 |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=106–119 |doi=10.1080/00934690.2019.1697018 |s2cid=213682801 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00934690.2019.1697018 |access-date=11 May 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Flakes can be used to create spear points and blades or knives.<ref name="Holdaway2012" /> Grindstones were used against grass seeds to make flour for bread, and to produce [[bone marrow|marrow]] from bones.<ref name="Grindstones2021" />

Stone artefacts not only were used for a range of necessary activities such as hunting, but they also hold a special spiritual meaning.<ref name="Brown2019">{{cite journal|last1=Brown|first1=Steve|year=2019|title=Aboriginal stone artefacts and Country: dynamism, new meanings, theory, and heritage|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/03122417.2019.1738667|journal=Australian Archaeology|volume=85|issue=3|pages=256–266|doi=10.1080/03122417.2019.1738667|s2cid=216270853|access-date=14 April 2021|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Indigenous Australians describe a stone artefact as holding the spirit of an ancestor who once owned it.<ref name="Brown2019" /> 30,000-year-old grinding stones have been found at Cuddie Springs, NSW.<ref name="Grindstones2021" /> Leilira blades from [[Arnhem Land]] were collected between 1931 and 1948 and are {{as of|lc=yes |2021}} held at the [[Australian Museum]].<ref name="Leilira2021" />

== Coolamons and carriers ==
[[Coolamon (vessel)|Coolamons]] are Aboriginal vessels, generally used to carry water, food, and to cradle babies.<ref name="Coolamons2021">{{cite web |title=Australian Aboriginal Carrying Vessels – Coolamons |url=https://joyofmuseums.com/museums/australasia-museums/australian-museums/museums-of-sydney/australian-museum/coolamons-aboriginal-carrying-vessel/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190405053812/https://joyofmuseums.com/museums/australasia-museums/australian-museums/museums-of-sydney/australian-museum/coolamons-aboriginal-carrying-vessel/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=5 April 2019 |website=Joy of Museums Virtual Tours |access-date=26 May 2021}}</ref> Coolamons could be made from a variety of materials including wood, bark, animal skin, stems, seed stalks, stolons, leaves and hair.<ref name="Pitman2012">{{cite journal |last1=Pitman |first1=H |last2=Wallis |first2=L |title=The Point of Spinifex: Aboriginal uses of spinifex grasses in Australia |journal=Ethnobotany Research and Applications |date=2012 |volume=10 |pages=109–131 |doi=10.17348/era.10.0.109-131 |hdl=10125/23550 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> When travelling long distances, coolamons were carried on the head. [[Akartne]] was placed underneath the coolamon to support its weight. They could be made from possum hair, feathers, or twisted grass.<ref name="Coolamons2021" />

=== Findings ===
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Museum Collections
|-
| [[Australian Museum]] || [[File:Aboriginal Coolamons and Carriers.jpg|thumb|205x205px|Aboriginal Coolamons and Carriers from the Australian Museum collection]]

The Australian Museum holds a bark water carrying vessel originating from [[Flinders Island (Queensland)|Flinders Island]], Queensland in 1905. This coolamon is made from the bark shell of a [[eucalyptus]] tree trunk that has been burnt and smoothed with stone and shells in order to hold and store water. A water bag made from kangaroo skin was acquired by the Australian Museum in 1893. It originates from the Urania people of North-West, Queensland.<ref name="Coolamons2021" />

| [[South Australian Museum]] || The South Australian Museum holds a wooden coolamon collected in 1971 by Robert Edwards. == Message sticks ==

[[File:Nma-55792463-031-wm-vs1 o3 1100.jpg|thumb|205x205px|Message stick]]
[[Message stick]]s, also known as "talking-sticks", were used in Aboriginal communities to communicate invitations, declarations of war, news of death and so forth.<ref name="Kelly2020">{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=Piers |title=Australian message sticks: Old questions, new directions |journal=Journal of Material Culture |date=2020 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=133–152 |doi=10.1177/1359183519858375 |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/1359183519858375 |access-date=26 May 2021|hdl=21.11116/0000-0003-FDF8-9 |s2cid=198687425 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Matthews1897">{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=Henry |title=Message-Sticks Used by the Aborigines of Australia |journal=American Anthropologist |date=1897 |volume=10 |pages=288–298 }}</ref> They were made of wood and were usually flat with motifs engraved on all sides to express a message. The type of wood and shape of a message stick could be a part of the message. Special messengers would carry message sticks over long distances and were able to travel through tribal borders without harm. After the message had been received, generally the message stick would be burned.<ref name="CultureVictoria2021">{{cite web |title=Message Stick |url=https://cv.vic.gov.au/stories/aboriginal-culture/the-aboriginal-object-collection-at-dunkeld-museum/message-stick/message-stick-1/ |website=cv.vic.gov.au |publisher=Culture Victoria |access-date=26 May 2021}}</ref>

== Ornamental artefacts ==
Some Aboriginal peoples used materials such as teeth and bone to make ornamental objects such as necklaces and headbands.<ref name="Akerman2018">{{cite book |last1=Akerman |first1=K |chapter=The esoteric and decorative use of bone, shell, and teeth in Australia. |title=The Archaeology of Portable Art |date=2018 |pages=199–219 |doi=10.4324/9781315299112-13 |isbn=978-1-315-29911-2 |url=https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315299112-13 |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>

=== Teeth ornaments ===
The most common teeth ornaments consisted of lower [[incisor]]s of [[Macropodidae|macropods]] such as [[kangaroo]]s or [[Wallaby|wallabies]]. One of the most fascinating discoveries was a necklace made from 178 [[Tasmanian devil]] (Sarcophilus harrisii) teeth recovered from Lake Nitchie in New South Wales in 1969. Forehead ornaments have also been found to use [[porpoise]] and [[dolphin]] teeth from the [[Gulf of Carpentaria]]. [[Crocodile]] teeth were used mainly in [[Arnhem Land]].<ref name="Akerman2018" />

=== Bone ornaments ===
Bones were often used for ornamental purposes, especially necklaces and [[pendant]]s. These were usually worn in association with ritual or age status but could also be worn casually. Bone ornaments found from [[Boulia]] in central western Queensland were made from the [[phalange]]s of kangaroos and [[dingo]]es. Branchiostegal rays of eels from the [[Tully River]] were used as pendant units by the [[Gulngay]] people. In western Victoria, [[echidna]] (Tachyglossus aculeatus) quills were threaded as necklaces. A pendant made from goose down, shells, a duck beak and the upper beak of a black swan was discovered from the [[Murray River]] in South Australia.  Talons of eagles were incorporated into ornaments among the [[Arrernte people|Arrernte]] of Central Australia. [[Wombat]] (Vombatus ursinus) claw necklaces are known from [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].<ref name="Akerman2018" /> Painted [[requiem shark]] [[vertebrae]] necklaces have been found in western Arnhem Land.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wright |first1=Duncan |last2=Langley |first2=Michelle |last3=May |first3=Sally |last4=Johnston |first4=Iain |last5=Allen |first5=Lindy |title=Painted shark vertebrae beads from the Djawumbu–Madjawarrnja complex, western Arnhem Land |journal=Australian Archaeology |date=2016 |volume=82 |pages=43–54 |doi=10.1080/03122417.2016.1164356 |hdl=1885/152750 |s2cid=151906011 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/03122417.2016.1164356 |access-date=11 May 2021|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Pearl shells===
Riji are the pearl shells traditionally worn by Aboriginal men in the north-west part of Australia, around present day [[Broome, Western Australia|Broome]]. The word ''riji'' is from the [[Bardi language]]. Another word for it is  ''jakuli''. Before being decorated, the pearl shell is known as ''guwan''. Lines known as ''ramu'', often in a sacred pattern or depicting a traditional story, are carved onto the guwan, at which point it becomes a riji. [[Ochre]] is sometimes applied to the incisions, for colour.   Riji are associated with water, as well as spiritual or healing powers, and life.<ref name=wam>{{cite web | title=Guwan | website=[[Western Australian Museum]] | date=2016 | url=http://museum.wa.gov.au/explore/lustre-online-text-panels/guwan | access-date=4 December 2020}}</ref>

===Kopis===
The Kopi [[mourning]] cap is an item of [[headware]] made from clay, worn by mostly womenfolk of some Aboriginal peoples, for up to six months after the death of a loved one. After cutting off their hair, they would weave a net using [[sinew]]s from [[emu]], place this on their head, and cover it with layers of [[gypsum]], a type of white [[clay]] obtained from rivers. They could be heavy (up to {{cvt|7|kg}}), and were sometimes worn by men.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kopi Workshop – Building an understanding of grief from an Indigenous cultural perspective | website=[[Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences]] | date=11 February 2017 | url=https://www.maas.museum/event/kopi/ | access-date=15 July 2021}}</ref> When the mourning period was over, the Kopi would be placed on the grave of the deceased person.<ref name="The Australian Museum">{{cite web | title=Mourning - Indigenous Australia| website=australian.museum | url=https://australian.museum/about/history/exhibitions/death-the-last-taboo/mourning-indigenous-australia/| date=22 November 2018 | access-date=15 July 2021}}</ref>

Other names for the Kopi were widow's cap, korno, mulya, mung-warro, pa-ta, and yúgarda.<ref name="The Australian Museum"/>

== Children's toys ==
Children's toys made by Aboriginal peoples were not only to entertain but also to educate.<ref name="Dender2015">{{cite journal |last1=Dender |first1=A |last2=Stagnitti |first2=K |title=Children's play in the Australian Indigenous context: the need for a contemporary view |journal=International Journal of Play |date=2015 |volume=1 |pages=3–16 |doi=10.1080/21594937.2014.977036 |s2cid=144424623 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/21594937.2014.977036 |access-date=11 May 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Toys were made from different materials depending on location and materials available.<ref name="Aboriginaltoys2021">{{cite web |last1=Fisher |first1=Rebecca |title=Aboriginal Toys |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/aboriginal-toys/?gclid=Cj0KCQjwutaCBhDfARIsAJHWnHunPBsQYM6o0-evWa-9ycw6re-DoN6LTUjOwP_4lOiCRoVfWdLd4sgaArHQEALw_wcB |website=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>

=== Dolls ===
"Dolls" could be made from cassia nemophila, with its branches assembled with string and grass. Features were often painted with clay to represent a baby.<ref name="Haagen1994">{{cite book |last1=Haagen |first1=C |title=Bush toys: Aboriginal children at play |date=1994 |publisher=Aboriginal Studies Press for the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies |location=Canberra }}</ref> Dolls made from [[Xanthorrhoea]] are called Kamma dolls and are from [[Keppel Island]]. Shell dolls could also be made from conical shells and were often wrapped in fabric to distinguish age or status.<ref name="Dolls2021">{{cite web |title=Dolls |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/aboriginal-toys/indigenous-australian-dolls |website=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="Akerman2018" />

=== Rattles ===
[[toy rattle|Rattles]] could be made out of a variety of different materials which would depend on geographical accessibility. For example, they could be made out of [[land snail]] shells, [[sea snail]] shells (''Haliotis asinina''), valves of [[scallop]] (''Annachlamys flabellata''), walnut seeds or olive shells which were strung together with string or hair and were often painted.<ref name="Haagen1994" /><ref name="Rattles2021">{{cite web |title=Rattles |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/aboriginal-toys/toys-for-infants/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="Akerman2018" />

=== Bags and baskets ===
In Arnhem Land, the Gulf region of Queensland and Cape York, children’s bags and baskets were made from fibre twine.<ref name="Haagen1994" />

=== Toy spears and shields ===
Play spears, which were often blunt wooden spears, were used by boys in mock battles and throwing games.<ref name="Toyspears2021">{{cite web |title=Toy spears, spearthrowers and targets |url=https://australian.museum/learn/cultures/atsi-collection/aboriginal-toys/toy-spears-general/ |website=Australian Museum |access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>

== Sacred items ==
Artefacts sometimes regarded as sacred items and/or used in ceremonies include [[bullroarer]]s, [[didgeridoo]]s and carved boards called [[churinga]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

== Art ==
Most [[Indigenous Australian art|Aboriginal art]] is not considered  artefact, but often the designs in Aboriginal art are similar designs to those originally on sacred artefacts.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Papunya : a place made after the story : the beginnings of the Western Desert painting movement|last=Bardon, Geoff, 1940-|date=2004|publisher=Miegunyah Press|others=Bardon, James.|isbn=0-522-85110-X|location=Carlton, Vic.|oclc=59098931}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aboriginal-bark-paintings.com/aboriginal-dot-art/|title=Aboriginal Dot Art {{!}} sell Aboriginal Dot Art {{!}} meaning dots in Aboriginal Art|date=2018-11-28|website=Aboriginal Bark Paintings|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref>

==Keeping Places==
<!---Redirects target this section.--->
A Keeping Place (usually capitalised) is an Aboriginal community-managed place for the safekeeping of repatriated cultural material<ref>{{cite web|title=Keeping Places & Beyond: A reader| series= Building Cultural Futures in NSW|url=https://mgnsw.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/keeping_places_and_beyondnew2.pdf| date=2010–2011| author =Museums & Galleries NSW| access-date=29 September 2021}}</ref> or local cultural heritage items, cultural artefacts, art and/or knowledge.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Aboriginal Heritage Museum and Keeping Place | website=Aboriginal Heritage Office| date=18 August 2011| url=https://www.aboriginalheritage.org/museum/ | access-date=29 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Merkell | first=Helen | title=Aboriginal historian calls for 'Keeping Places' in NSW centres |website=ABC News | date=3 February 2016 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2016-02-03/aboriginal-historian-calls-for-keeping-places-in-nsw-centres/7135714 | access-date=29 September 2021}}</ref> Krowathunkooloong Keeping Place in [[Gippsland, Victoria]] is one example of a Keeping Place.<ref>{{cite web | title=Krowathunkooloong Keeping Place | website=Gippsland & East Gippsland Aboriginal Co-Operative Ltd. – GEGAC | url=https://www.gegac.org.au/keepingplace/ | access-date=29 September 2021}}</ref> In [[Western Australia]] there is a collaboratively developed and managed online system for managing cultural heritage known as The Keeping Place Project.<ref >{{cite web | title=The Keeping Place Project | website=Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation| publisher = Australian Government | date=22 January 2020 | url=https://www.ilsc.gov.au/home/project-profiles/the-keeping-place-project/ | access-date=29 September 2021}}</ref>

extract: Australian Aboriginal artefacts include a variety of cultural artefacts used by Aboriginal Australians. Most Aboriginal artefacts were multi-purpose and could be used for a variety of different occupations. Spears, clubs, boomerangs and shields were used generally as weapons for hunting and in warfare. Watercraft technology artefacts in the form of dugout and bark canoes were used for transport and for fishing. Stone artefacts include cutting tools and grinding stones to hunt and make food. Coolamons and carriers such as dillybags, allowed Aboriginal peoples to carry water, food and cradle babies. Message sticks were used for communication, and ornamental artefacts for decorative and ceremonial purposes. Aboriginal children’s toys were used to both entertain and educate.
